key: Yea, many a woman is more firm and better than the man who turns Away from Gods, and offers not.
s: In a hymn mixing praise of the Maruts with thanks to patrons, the verse follows a blessing on a woman; Sāyaṇa, on 5.61.6, takes her as Śaśīyasī, King Taranta’s queen, and the man as a miser who neither praises the gods nor gives.

evidence.words: चतसृणां शशीयसी नाम तरन्तस्य राज्ञो भार्या देवता … शशीयसी इस्येतन्महिष्या नाम। सैव "स्त्री । यद्वा । उतेत्ययमेवकारार्थे । स्त्रीषु सैव प्रशस्येत्यर्थः । त्वसमसिमनेमेत्यनुच्चानि ' इति वचनात् त्वेति निघातः ॥ सैव “पुंसः पुरुषात् “वस्यसी वसीयसी “भवति । कस्मात्पुंस इत्युच्यते । “अदेवत्रात् । देवाः अनेन त्रायन्ते स्तुत्यादिना सः देवत्रः । न देवत्रः अदेवत्रः। तस्मात् “अराधसः । राधो धनम् । दानार्हधनरहितात् । लुब्धकादित्यर्थः ॥
evidence.gloss: Of the four verses the deity is Śaśīyasī, wife of King Taranta. … Śaśīyasī is the queen’s name; she is the woman. Or uta means ‘only’: among women she alone is praiseworthy. She is better than the man: than the adevatra (one by whom the gods are not served with praise and the like), than the arādhas (without wealth fit for giving), that is, than a greedy man.

reason: The problem holds: the name comes only from Sāyaṇa (Griffith’s day text for 5.61 names Taranta at 5.61.10 but not the queen), and his words spell it शशीयसी, Śaśīyasī; the batch gives other Sāyaṇa-only names with diacritics (Vāmadeva, Viśvavārā, Kaśyapa). Changed only that spelling; Taranta stays as Griffith’s day text prints it. Reopened packet.js veda 54: both evidence pieces re-found verbatim. verse.js ok [414,6]; entry-check ok. Commentator, reading, src and evidence unchanged.
